The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) namely Zn corrosion is determined by both kinetic and thermodynamic aspects. In the alkaline electrolyte, as shown in the Pourbaix diagram , the standard reduction voltage of Zn/ZnO( , -1.26 V vs SHE at pH of 14) is lower than that of the HER, , -0.83 V vs SHE at pH of 14). Therefore, the Zn corrosion reaction generation with hydrogen evolution is a spontaneous process driven by thermodynamics in alkaline circumstances . However, the practical HER in the alkaline electrolyte is also repressed by the kinetic and thermodynamic over-potential. The over-potential ( ) of HER on Zn anode was expressed by the Tafel equation , which demonstrated the influence of current density on the actual HER. Because the Zn metal belongs to the high hydrogen over-potential metals (for example, the over-potential of HER on the pure Zn metal is -1.76 V vs. Hg/HgO). the catalytic activity of Zn for HER was too inferior, when the Zn can be utilized as catalyst for water splitting leading to the inhibition of hydrogen evolution on Zn surface . However, the over-potential of HER on the ZnO increases to -1.399 V vs. Hg/HgO. In other words, the HER would be boosted when the ZnO byproduct formation on the surface of Zn anodes. Besides, owing to the hydrogen evolution, the Coulombic efficiency of alkaline Zn batteries cannot be 100% because the electrons are partly snatched by H2. Whats more, in a sealed battery, the generated hydrogen will aggrandize the internal pressure and even lead to explosions of the sealed battery.

The cyclic and powerful ability of electric vehicles was increased by the use of LIBs based on aqueous electrolytes. They can deliver high energy density and power density and are widely used in watches, LED screens, and many other applications. In aqueous lithium-ion batteries (ALIBs), the concentrated saline solution acts as an electrolyte that aids the transfer of Li-ions among electrodes and produces electric current. In contrast to organic electrolytes (which consists of an organic solvent and a lithium salt) and non-aqueous electrolytes (organic or inorganic solvent), ALIBs are cost-effective, non-flammable, and do not have the risk of an explosion. However, the electrochemical stability window of ALIBs is limited to 1.23 V voltage, along with a much smaller energy density compared to non-aqueous LIBs. So, there was a need to develop an electrolyte that not only enhances the electrochemical performance but also solves the safety issues related to the operation of batteries. The aqueous electrolyte can be classified into water-in-salt (WIS) electrolytes. The WIS electrolyte shows the stable electrochemical window and low chemical activity of water, and suppressing hydrolysis side reactions. WIS electrolytes improve the electrochemical stability of the battery up to 3 V. The performance of WIS electrolytes can also be enhanced through an increase in electrolyte concentration up to saturation. This electrolyte saturation result in the formation of a solid SEI. The use of the SEI-forming additive (sulfone, carbonate, cyclic sulfate) helps in the stabilization of electrolytes even at high-energy cathode surfaces.

In recent years, there has been an unprecedented shift in energy utilization towards renewable sources of energy. Also, the rapid growth of environmental concerns, the degradation of fossil fuels, and the rising energy demand have led to a significant increase in environmental concerns and energy demands over the last few decades. Therefore, the development of perpetual and high-performance energy storage/conversion systems has accelerated. Supercapacitors (SCs) have attracted considerable attention among the various energy storage technologies because of their fast charging-discharging capability, high power density, and negligible safety risks. Because of its beneficial properties, SCs have become widely used in portable electronic devices and hybrid electric vehicles. SCs will require significantly increased energy density to become widely used because of their limited potential window and capacitive performance. The use of a hybrid paradigm, such as a supercapacitor is one of the most popular methods used to increase energy density. This involves combining capacitive electrode materials (activated carbon) with battery-type electrode materials (metal oxides). Using the synergistic properties of these electrodes, a supercapacitor could provide high energy density while maintaining rate capability, cycle life, or power density. The use of electrode materials with intrinsic synergistic properties will likely play a significant role in enhancing the energy storage performance of supercapacitors.

Because of their large surface area and flaky architecture, the fabricated electrodes allowed electrolyte ions to diffuse into the interior of the electrodes rapidly. Therefore, their electrochemical performance was enhanced because of their large active channels. The ASC device exhibited remarkable energy storage performance when constructed using Ni-ZIF/Ni-B-24 h//AC(positive/negative electrodes) in addition to its superior charge storage properties. The device attains a maximum energy density of 46.6 Wh kg-1 at a power density of 1600 W kg-1 and maintains 28.8 Wh kg-1 at a power density of 8000 W kg-1. Furthermore, after 5000 long cycles, the device demonstrated cycle life with a high coulombic efficiency of 99.2 %. Two-dimensional ultrathin nanosheets are responsible for this electrochemical performance because of their large quantity of accessible surface area and active sites, accelerated diffusion, and charge transfer ability. Because of the simplicity and convenience of this method, this study could catalyze the development of MOF-based electrodes for energy storage in the future.

Consequently, the ZMO:5 Co PNCs electrode showed superior electrochemical properties in terms of high Cs value, good rate capability and excellent cycle life. From the impressive high energy density of the pouch-type HSC device, the red and green LEDs operated with a potential window of 1.45 V. Various power batteries including lead-acid , nickel metal hydride  and lithium-ion (Li-ion) are available for electric vehicles applications. In general, the performance of power batteries directly affects the performance of electric vehicles . However, the heat generated from the power battery during charge/discharge can lead to safety risks such as overheating, combustion, and explosion of the battery . Ramadass et al. did a capacity fade analysis for Li-ion battery and elucidated that 31% and 36% of the initial capacity were lost after 800 charge-discharge cycles which were operated at 25 °C and 45 °C, respectively; while the capacity fades were more than 60% after 600 cycles at 50 °C and 70% after 500 cycles at 55 °C. Li and Su also pointed out that the cycle life of lithium-ion battery is 3323 cycles at 45 °C, but 1037 cycles at 60 °C. Therefore, thermal safety is a key issue for the research and development of power battery within electric vehicles. The present study investigated the effects of ionic conductivity and electronic conductivity on the performance of NCM cathodes. Specifically, two groups of electrodes with similar ionic or electronic conductivities were fabricated by adjusting the electrode composition and density. Through pulse polarization measurements, we determined that electronic conductivity, associated with the IR-drop, plays a dominant role at low C-rates, whereas ionic conductivity, related to Li+ kinetics, becomes increasingly critical at high C-rates. Rate capability tests revealed that electrodes with similar ionic conductivities exhibited smaller capacity differences at high C-rates than electrodes with similar electronic conductivities, underscoring the importance of Li+ transport kinetics at high C-rates. This conclusion was further confirmed by the results of DVA and cyclic voltammetry. Additionally, cycling for over 300 cycles at low C-rate was performed to compare the long-term cycle life of the electrodes in the two groups. Electrodes with similar ionic conductivities showed varying discharge capacity retention, whereas electrodes with similar electronic conductivities exhibited consistent discharge capacity retention, emphasizing the critical role of electronic conductivity at low C-rates. Furthermore, insufficient electronic conductivity led to the formation of microcracks within the particles, facilitating electrolyte infiltration and triggering side reactions that ultimately degraded the cycle life. These degradation mechanisms were visually confirmed through CP-SEM and further verified using SSRM and ex situ XRD analyses. Our results provide valuable insights into the distinct roles of ionic conductivity and electronic conductivity on the electrochemical performances, offering a foundation for designing cells with specific performance.

Two different phases, abusively called polymorphs , have been reported for the cathode material with the chemical formula "LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4”. A low temperature ordered structure with P4332 space group can be obtained by synthesis in oxygen atmosphere or post-annealing in air below 700 °C . In this structure the Li atoms are located at 8c sites, Ni atoms at 4 a sites, Mn atoms at 12 d sites, and O atoms at 8 c and 24 e sites. For synthesis routes employing higher synthesis temperature (over 700 °C) a "LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4” phase with Fd-3 m structure is obtained . This high temperature phase is always accompanied with a rocksalt impurity, which has been attributed either to NixO , LixNi1-xO , or (LiNiMn)xO , and concomitant to the presence of oxygen deficiency . A similar oxygen evolution is also observed for another spinel, Li1±yMn2O4-type materials, and which occurrence impacts on the charge/discharge voltage profiles and the structural mechanism during cycling . Within the Fd-3m structure, Ni and Mn atoms are randomly distributed at 16d sites. X-ray diffraction (XRD) does not allow distinguishing these two structures because of the closeness of the Ni and Mn atomic scattering factors.
